t.2.19.1: Then him, downcast with anguish and exceedingly indignant, hissing like a lord of serpents, his eyes dilated with rage...
t.2.19.2: Approaching Saumitri, his dear brother and friend, the self-possessed Rāma, holding his spirit steady with fortitude, spoke these words.
t.2.19.3: O Saumitri, let that same eager bustle of preparations which was mine for the sake of the consecration now be for the sake of calling off the consecration.
t.2.19.4: Act in such a way that our mother, whose mind is tormented over my consecration, may not remain full of misgiving.
t.2.19.5: O Saumitri, I cannot bear to disregard even for a moment the anguish that has arisen in her mind, this sickness of suspicion.
t.2.19.6: I do not recall ever having done here even the slightest thing displeasing to my mothers or to my father, whether knowingly or unknowingly.
t.2.19.7: May my father, who is truthful, true to his promises, and ever truly valorous, and who is afraid out of fear of the other world, be free from fear.
t.2.19.8: For if this undertaking were left unaccomplished, he too would suffer anguish of mind, thinking, “My word has not proved true,” and his anguish would torment me as well.
t.2.19.9: Therefore, Lakṣmaṇa, setting aside the arrangements for the consecration, I wish to go forth from here to the forest without delay.
t.2.19.10: Today, through my banishment, the king's daughter will have attained her aim; then she will, undisturbed, have her son Bharata consecrated.
t.2.19.11: When I, wearing bark garments and deerskin and bearing a mass of matted locks, have gone to the forest, Kaikeyī will have happiness of mind.
t.2.19.12: That by which this resolve has been formed and the mind so firmly settled, I ought not to trouble; I shall go forth into exile without delay.
t.2.19.14: For how could Kaikeyī have resolved upon tormenting me, were this disposition of hers not divine, ordained by Fate?
t.2.19.13: O Saumitri, it is Fate alone that must be seen at work in my banishment, and in the taking back once more of the kingdom that had been granted to me.
t.2.19.15: For you know, gentle one, that I have never made any distinction among my mothers, nor has she ever shown any difference between me and her own son.
t.2.19.16: As for her fierce words, so hard to utter, aimed at halting my consecration and at sending me into exile, I can ascribe them to nothing other than fate.
t.2.19.17: How could she, a princess endowed with a noble nature and possessed of such virtues, speak words to my hurt like a common woman in the presence of her husband?
t.2.19.18: But that which is inconceivable is fate, and it is not overcome even among living beings; clearly a reversal has befallen both me and her.
t.2.19.20: Pleasure and pain, fear and anger, gain and loss, birth and death: whatever of this kind befalls anyone, surely that is the work of fate.
t.2.19.19: What man, O Saumitri, can dare to fight against fate, which cannot be grasped in any way except through its workings?
t.2.19.21: Even though my consecration has been obstructed, I feel no distress; therefore you too, being free from distress and following my lead, must quickly withdraw the preparations for the consecration rite.
t.2.19.22: Lakṣmaṇa, our younger mother is not to be greatly suspected in this obstacle to my kingship, for those seized by fate speak what is unwelcome, and you know that fate is of such power.
